strengths: First near-optimal sample complexity bounds for constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs) with a generative model, addressing an important theoretical gap in constrained RL.

Establishes a provable statistical separation between relaxed feasibility (achieving $\tilde{O}(SA(B+H)/\epsilon^2)$ without polynomial dependence on the Slater margin $\zeta$) and strict feasibility (achieving $\tilde{\Theta}(SA(B+H)/(\epsilon^2\zeta^2))$).

Technically sophisticated analysis combining a model-based primal-dual framework, reward perturbation to induce uniform action gaps, row-decoupling state-action absorbing constructions, and an instance-dependent Bernstein variance hierarchy.

Comprehensive lower bounds: establishes an adaptive minimax lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(SAH/(\epsilon^2\zeta^2))$ for weakly communicating CAMDPs with span $H = \Theta(D)$, and a matching transient-time lower bound $\tilde{\Omega}(SAB/(\epsilon^2\zeta^2))$ under balanced sampling.
The manuscript and appendix are mathematically rigorous, clearly organized, and well-written.
weaknesses: The upper bound results rely on Assumption 1 (Policy-wise discounted variance condition). While the authors show that this condition holds on their hard instances, they do not prove that it holds universally for all CAMDPs satisfying the bias span and transient time bounds, leaving open whether the upper bound applies unconditionally across all instances.

The transient-time lower bound (Theorem 7 / Section F) is established only under the balanced generative model protocol (uniform sampling across state-action pairs), whereas the weakly communicating lower bound (Theorem 6) allows adaptive sampling. Extending the $B$-dependent lower bound to adaptive sampling would strengthen the lower bound theory.

The work is entirely theoretical and does not include empirical validation or simulations illustrating the practical performance, convergence, or sensitivity to hyperparameters (such as the perturbation parameter $\omega$ and discretization grid $\Lambda$).

strengths: First near-optimal sample complexity characterization for constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs) under a generative model, addressing an open problem that bridges unconstrained AMDPs and discounted CMDPs.

Establishes a sharp statistical separation between relaxed feasibility (achieving O~(SA(B + H) / epsilon^2), free of polynomial Slater margin dependence) and strict feasibility (requiring O~(SA(B + H) / (epsilon^2 zeta^2))).

Provides matching lower bounds: an adaptive minimax lower bound Omega~(SAH / (epsilon^2 zeta^2)) for weakly communicating CAMDPs and a balanced transient lower bound Omega~(SAB / (epsilon^2 zeta^2)), proving that the zeta^(-2) penalty for strict feasibility is unavoidable.

Technically sophisticated analysis: introduces a cross-signal concentration argument using randomized reward perturbations, row-decoupled absorbing MDP constructions, and a Bernstein hierarchy to avoid paying an exponential union bound over the deterministic policy class.
The manuscript is clearly written, mathematically rigorous, and provides comprehensive, self-contained proofs.
weaknesses: The upper bound guarantees rely on Assumption 1 (a policy-wise discounted variance condition). Although the authors prove that their lower bound constructions satisfy this condition, the manuscript would benefit from a deeper discussion of the universal validity or scope of this assumption across general multichain CAMDPs.

The algorithm is computationally demanding, requiring the exact solution of an empirical discounted MDP at each primal-dual iteration for T = O~(epsilon^(-4)) (or O~(epsilon^(-2) zeta^(-4))) steps; while the primary focus is sample complexity, discussing computational aspects would improve completeness.

The B-dependent transient lower bound is currently established under the balanced sampling model rather than fully adaptive sampling, leaving a minor gap in lower bound generality for general multichain instances.

strengths: First near-optimal finite-sample complexity guarantees for constrained average-reward MDPs (CAMDPs) with access to a generative model, addressing an important theoretical gap between discounted CMDPs and unconstrained AMDPs.

Comprehensive coverage of both relaxed feasibility and strict feasibility regimes, showing a provable separation in the dependence on the Slater margin (dimensionless in relaxed feasibility vs. 1/zeta^2 in strict feasibility).
Near-matching lower bounds: an adaptive minimax lower bound for weakly communicating CAMDPs scaling with H, and a transient-time lower bound scaling with B under balanced sampling.
Rigorous cross-signal concentration argument (Theorem 2) using state-action row absorption and Bernstein hierarchies to avoid loose union bounds over the exponential deterministic policy class.
Thorough and mathematically complete manuscript with full derivations, explicit LP separation calculations, and variance verification on hard instances.
weaknesses: The upper bound guarantees rely critically on Assumption 1 (policy-wise discounted variance condition). While the authors verify this condition on their hard instance constructions, the paper does not establish whether Assumption 1 holds universally for all CAMDPs with parameters B and H or characterize how restrictive it is in general.

The transient lower bound (Theorem 7) is restricted to balanced generative-model sampling protocols, whereas the weakly communicating lower bound (Theorem 6) holds for fully adaptive generative models.
Computational complexity is high: Algorithm 1 requires solving an empirical discounted MDP at each primal-dual iteration for T = O(1/eps^4) (relaxed) or O(1/(eps^2 zeta^4)) (strict) steps.

The algorithm outputs an external mixture of stationary deterministic policies rather than a single stationary randomized policy; while standard for multichain CAMDPs, further discussion on the practical execution and planning trade-offs would improve the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem in reinforcement learning theory: characterizing the sample complexity of learning in constrained average-reward Markov decision processes (CAMDPs) with a generative model.

The formulation considers both relaxed and strict feasibility settings and attempts to establish the dependency on structural parameters such as the bias span $H$, transient time bound $B$, and Slater parameter $\zeta$.
weaknesses: Unsupported upper bound sample complexity: The paper claims an upper bound of $\tilde{O}(\frac{SA(B+H)}{\varepsilon^2})$, but the derivation relies on reducing the AMDP to a discounted MDP with effective discount factor $1 - \gamma = \Theta(\frac{\varepsilon}{B+H})$ and directly invoking Lemma 13 (from Vaswani et al., 2022). In standard discounted CMDP bounds (including Vaswani et al., 2022), the sample complexity scales as $(1-\gamma)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2}$. Substituting $1-\gamma = \Theta(\frac{\varepsilon}{B+H})$ yields a sample complexity on the order of $\frac{(B+H)^3}{\varepsilon^5}$, not $\frac{B+H}{\varepsilon^2}$. The authors do not develop any variance-reduction or average-reward Bernstein concentration mechanisms to bridge this polynomial gap, instead simply asserting on pages 18 and 20 that $N \ge \tilde{O}(\frac{SA(B+H)}{\varepsilon^2})$ suffices.

Confusion between per-pair and total sample complexity: In Section 3 and Algorithm 1, $N$ is defined as the number of samples collected for each state-action pair $(s, a)$. However, in Theorems 2 and 3, $N$ is set to $\tilde{O}(\frac{SA(B+H)}{\varepsilon^2})$. If $N$ samples are drawn per $(s, a)$, the total sample complexity across all $S \times A$ pairs would be $\tilde{O}(\frac{S^2 A^2(B+H)}{\varepsilon^2})$, directly contradicting the main claims in the abstract and introduction.

Fatal circular definition of parameters: In Section 5 and Theorem 3 (pages 7 and 20), the algorithm parameters are defined circularly. The discount factor is set as $\gamma = 1 - \frac{\varepsilon_{opt}}{4(B+H)}$, while $\varepsilon_{opt}$ is defined as $\frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)\zeta}{200}$. Substituting $\varepsilon_{opt}$ into the expression for $1-\gamma$ gives $1-\gamma = \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)\zeta}{800(B+H)}$, which cancels $1-\gamma$ and enforces the identity $1 = \frac{\varepsilon\zeta}{800(B+H)}$. This circular dependence invalidates the algorithmic specification.

Severe mathematical fallacy in Theorem 4's lower bound: In Appendix G (page 29), the proof constructs an instance with diameter $D$ to obtain an $\tilde{\Omega}(\frac{SAD}{\varepsilon^2 \zeta^2})$ bound, and then claims: 'by noting that the bias span $H$ is always bounded above by the diameter $D$, this implies a corresponding lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(\frac{SAH}{\varepsilon^2 \zeta^2})$'. This is a basic logical reversal: since $H \le D$, a lower bound scaling with $D$ does not imply a lower bound scaling with $H$.

Flawed lower bound proof in Theorem 5: In Appendix F, the hard instance (Figure 4) contains absorbing states (states 2, 3, 4, 5), violating the communicating / weakly communicating assumption claimed in the theorem. Furthermore, the Fano's inequality calculation on page 28 bounds the required samples by $n \ge \tilde{\Omega}(\frac{B \log(SA)}{\varepsilon^2 \zeta^2})$, but the authors then abruptly substitute $SA(B+H)$ in place of $B \log(SA)$ without any derivation, artificially creating the claimed lower bound.

Algorithmic inconsistency: Algorithm 1 inputs and computes a discount factor $\gamma$ (lines 1 and 4), yet line 8 instructs the solver to compute the Blackwell-optimal policy of an unconstrained average-reward MDP $(\hat{P}, r_p + \lambda_t c)$. The paper repeatedly contradicts itself on whether the inner solver solves a discounted MDP or an AMDP.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely theoretical problem: characterizing the minimax sample complexity of constrained average-reward Markov decision processes (CAMDPs) with a generative model.
The conceptual formulation addressing both relaxed feasibility (allowing small constraint violations) and strict feasibility (zero constraint violation) is well-motivated.
The paper is ambitious in attempting to connect transient time bounds, bias span, and Slater conditions into unified finite-sample bounds.
weaknesses: Critical technical flaw in the upper bound derivation: In the proofs of Theorem 2 (Section B, page 18) and Theorem 3 (Section C, page 20), the algorithm reduces the AMDP to a discounted MDP with discount factor $\gamma = 1 - \frac{\varepsilon_{opt}}{4(B+H)}$ and invokes Lemma 13 (from Vaswani et al., 2022). Lemma 13 states that the error is bounded by $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{C(\delta)}{N(1-\gamma)^3}}\right)$. To make this value at most $B+H$ (as required by Lemma 11), one requires $N \ge \Omega\left(\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^3 (B+H)^2}\right) = \Omega\left(\frac{B+H}{\varepsilon_{opt}^3}\right)$. This yields an $\varepsilon^{-3}$ sample complexity. However, the authors arbitrarily claim on page 18 that $N \ge \tilde{O}\left(\frac{SA(B+H)}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$. The claimed $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate does not follow from the lemmas invoked.

Confusion regarding sample complexity per state-action pair vs. total sample complexity: In Algorithm 1 and Section 3, $N$ is defined as the number of samples collected for each state-action pair. Yet in Theorems 2 and 3, $N$ is stated as $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{SA(B+H)}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$. If $N$ samples are drawn per state-action pair, the total sample complexity would be $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{S^2 A^2 (B+H)}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, which contradicts the main claims in the Abstract and Introduction.

Mathematically incorrect mixture policy assertion: In Theorem 1 (page 14, lines 15–16), the paper defines the output policy $\hat{\pi} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \hat{\pi}_t$ and asserts that $\rho^{\hat{\pi}} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \rho^{\hat{\pi}_t}$. In infinite-horizon MDPs, the average reward and stationary distribution are non-linear functions of the policy parameters. Averaging the stochastic policy transition kernels does not result in the average of their stationary rewards.

Unsound proof of Lemma 17: In Appendix E (page 24), the proof asserts that because $T^\pi$ is a non-expansion, the bias error satisfies $\|h^\star - \hat{h}\|_\infty \le D \|\delta\|_\infty$. For average-reward Bellman equations, the operator $I - P_\pi$ is singular and non-invertible, so bias perturbations cannot be bounded by simple contraction arguments without analyzing the fundamental matrix / Drazin inverse.

Unsound proof of Lemma 18: The estimation of the transient time bound $B$ assumes trajectories are stopped upon reaching the recurrent class $R^\pi$. In an unknown MDP, the learner does not know which states are recurrent. Furthermore, $B$ is defined as the supremum over all deterministic policies ($A^S$ policies), but the proof only bounds the sample complexity for a single fixed policy.

Flawed lower bound constructions and missing proofs: In Theorem 5, the lower bound is stated for communicating CAMDPs, but the construction in Figure 4 contains four absorbing states (states 2, 3, 4, and 5), making the instance strictly non-communicating. In addition, the transition probabilities out of state 0 in Figure 4 are invalid (summing to $2 - 2/B > 1$). Finally, the proof of Theorem 4 in Appendix G is entirely absent—it consists of a few descriptive paragraphs and concludes with a Q.E.D. symbol without any formal mathematical derivation, KL divergence calculations, or Fano's inequality application.
Redundant figures: Figures 1 and 2 in the main text are duplicated verbatim as Figures 5 and 6 in Appendix G, and Figure 3 is duplicated verbatim as Figure 4 in Appendix F.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely theoretical problem: characterizing the minimax sample complexity of constrained average-reward Markov decision processes (CAMDPs) under a generative model.
The conceptual separation between relaxed feasibility and strict feasibility is well-motivated and parallels recent developments in discounted CMDPs.
weaknesses: Fatal Flaw in Sample Complexity Derivation (Order of ε): The paper claims an upper bound of O~(SA(B+H)/ε^2). However, in Appendix B and D, the reduction from average-reward to discounted MDPs chooses 1 - γ = Θ(ε / (B+H)) (Lemma 11), requiring the discounted value estimation error to be bounded by B + H. The paper then applies Lemma 13 (taken from Vaswani et al., 2022), where the estimation error is O(sqrt(1 / (N(1-γ)^3))). Setting sqrt(1 / (N(1-γ)^3)) <= B + H requires N >= Ω((B+H) / ε^3), not ε^2. On page 18, the authors omit the algebraic calculation and simply write down N >= O~(SA(B+H)/ε^2), hiding the fact that their derivation actually yields an ε^3 dependence.

Circular Parameter Definitions: In Section 5 and Appendix C (Theorem 3 and its proof), the discount factor is set as γ = 1 - ε_opt / (4(B+H)), while ε_opt is simultaneously defined as ε_opt = ε(1-γ)ζ / 200. This is a circular definition (1 - γ ∝ ε_opt ∝ 1 - γ) that implies 1 = εζ / (800(B+H)), which cannot hold for arbitrary problem parameters.

Disconnect Between Algorithm 1 and Theoretical Analysis: Algorithm 1 sets a discount factor γ in Line 4, but γ is never used anywhere in the algorithm. In Line 8, the algorithm solves an empirical unconstrained average-reward MDP. However, the theoretical analysis directly cites Lemmas 13 and 14 from Vaswani et al. (2022), which were specifically established for algorithms that solve empirical discounted MDPs. There is no proof that the policy output by solving empirical AMDPs satisfies the concentration guarantees of Vaswani et al. (2022).

Unsound Bounds on Empirical Bias Span: In Lemma 11, the empirical bias span is bounded as H_hat <= 2H by citing Lemma 17. However, Lemma 17 only discusses estimating the bias span of the true optimal policy. It does not prove that an empirical transition matrix P_hat constructed from finite samples preserves the weak communicating property or has a bias span bounded by 2H for arbitrary policies. In general, finite-sample empirical MDPs can easily have disconnected components or arbitrarily large bias spans.

Incomplete and Flawed Lower Bound Proofs: (1) The proof of Theorem 4 in Appendix G is incomplete: it never defines the transition probabilities, rewards, or constraints for the component MDP (x,y,z), provides no KL divergence calculations, and merely asserts the lower bound in words. (2) Theorems 4 and 5 do not specify that they only apply to the strict feasibility setting. Since Theorem 2 claims an upper bound of O~(SA(B+H)/ε^2) under relaxed feasibility (with no dependence on ζ), Theorems 4 and 5 as stated directly contradict Theorem 2. (3) The construction in Appendix F (Figure 4) contains absorbing states (states 2, 3, 4, 5), violating the communicating assumption under which Theorem 5 is stated.

Unrealistic Assumptions and Estimators: The definition of the bias span bound H := max_π ||h^π||_span requires all stationary policies to have uniformly bounded bias span, which is overly restrictive. Furthermore, Lemma 18 claims that the transient time B can be estimated by sampling trajectories until reaching recurrent states R^π; however, under unknown dynamics, the agent cannot know which states are recurrent.
